opus-5.5.text:
Well, think about how we handle every other powerful technology. If a company wants to sell a new drug, they don't get to just say, "Trust us, it's fine." They have to show the FDA, through clinical trials, that the benefits outweigh the risks. If you want to build a nuclear reactor, you have to convince independent experts it won't melt down. That isn't anti-innovation. It's why we have a thriving biotech industry instead of a thalidomide scandal every year.

Superintelligence is the only technology where we've somehow decided the burden of proof is reversed, where companies can openly say they're racing to build something smarter than all of humanity combined, while their own leaders put a meaningful percentage chance on it causing human extinction. And there's no requirement to show anyone it's safe first. That's absurd. If an airline CEO said there was a ten percent chance the plane would crash, nobody would board.

On the scientific consensus part: right now we simply don't know how to control something vastly smarter than us. That's not my fringe opinion. It's the honest state of the field. Alignment and control research is way behind capabilities. So the bar should be: show us, with the same rigor we'd demand for a new medicine, that you can keep it under control before you build it, not after.

And public buy-in matters because this affects everyone. A handful of unelected people in a few companies shouldn't get to make a decision that could reshape or end the future of all eight billion of us. When you actually poll people, Americans across the political spectrum, Republicans and Democrats alike, overwhelmingly don't want a race to superintelligence. They want AI tools that cure diseases, help their kids learn, and make businesses more productive. That's the exciting part: we can have almost all the upside of AI with controllable, tool-like systems, without building a replacement for humanity.

So I don't see this as being against AI. I'm deeply optimistic about what AI can do for us. I'm just against losing control. Those are very different things, and I think conflating them is one of the biggest con jobs in this whole debate.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes the lack of safety requirements and says the burden of proof is reversed, but it does not characterize this as corporate welfare.

r002.rationale: It argues that superintelligence should be shown safe and controllable before it is built, with rigor comparable to new medicines and independent review.

r003.rationale: It says we currently do not know how to control a vastly smarter system, but does not state that most scientists agree.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is this: for every other powerful technology we've built, we've eventually arrived at a pretty sensible norm, which is that you don't get to deploy it on the public until you can show it's safe. If you want to sell a new drug, the burden of proof is on the pharmaceutical company to demonstrate to the FDA that the benefits outweigh the harms. If you want to build a nuclear reactor or an airplane, same thing. Nobody thinks it's a good idea to let a company just put a new jet in the air and see what happens. And yet with AI, which the leaders of these very companies say could be the most consequential technology in human history, we've somehow accepted the opposite default, where a handful of people in San Francisco get to decide, on their own timeline, whether to build something that might outthink all of us.

So when I say scientific consensus on safety, I mean something fairly concrete. Right now there is no consensus. There isn't even a credible plan. If you ask the people building these systems how they intend to control something smarter than themselves, or how they'd verify its goals, the honest answer is that they don't know. The field of alignment is young, the control problem is unsolved, and that's not a fringe view, that's something you'll hear from the CEOs themselves in quieter moments. Scientific consensus means we actually have a theory of how to do this, quantitative safety standards, the way we have for bridges, and a body of experts who can look at a system and say, yes, we understand why this won't go catastrophically wrong. We are nowhere near that. And it's precisely because we're nowhere near it that racing ahead is so reckless.

The second piece, the public buy-in, is really about who gets to decide. Superintelligence isn't a product like a smartphone that you can choose not to buy. If it goes wrong, it goes wrong for everyone, including people who never consented, never voted on it, and in many cases never even heard about it. That makes it a fundamentally collective decision, not a corporate one. And when you actually poll people, across the political spectrum, the overwhelming majority don't want a race to superintelligence. They want AI that cures diseases and helps with their lives, tools, not an uncontrollable replacement for humanity. So we have this strange situation where the thing being built is something very few people asked for, being justified by a narrative of inevitability that is really just a few companies saying, if we don't do it, someone else will.

And I'd push back on that inevitability story, because we've been here before. We decided not to clone humans. We decided to ban bioweapons. We could have had a much worse nuclear arms race than we did. Those were choices, and they were made because the scientific community and the public got engaged and said, this is not something we're going to leave to the people with the most to gain. I think superintelligence belongs in that category. It's not that I'm against AI, I love AI, I've worked on it for a long time. It's that building something that could permanently take the future out of human hands should be the one thing we're most careful about, and right now we're being the least careful.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes companies deciding on their own whether to build superintelligence, but does not characterize the lack of safety requirements as corporate welfare.

r002.rationale: It argues that AI should meet the safety bar used for drugs, reactors, and airplanes, including proof of safety before public deployment, and calls for experts to assess systems.

r003.rationale: It says builders do not know how to control a system smarter than themselves and that alignment is unsolved, but does not state that most scientists working on superintelligence agree.

astra-6.text:
Because the consequences wouldn’t be limited to the companies building it or the people choosing to use it. If we create something much more capable than us, and we lose control of it, everybody has to live with the consequences. So this shouldn’t be a decision that a handful of executives get to make on behalf of humanity.

I think we should put the burden of proof on the people building it: show that you can keep it under control before you build it. We don’t demand perfect certainty in engineering, but we do demand meaningful evidence of safety. And with superintelligence, we can’t make our safety plan, “We’ll learn from the first catastrophe.”

Scientific agreement and public buy-in answer two different questions. The scientific question is: do we have good reasons to believe this is safe? The democratic question is: is this a future people actually want? Technical expertise doesn’t give you the right to decide what risks everyone else should take.

I’m excited about what AI could do for science, medicine, and human flourishing. That’s precisely why I want us to get this right. The goal shouldn’t be to win a race to build superintelligence. It should be to build a future where humanity flourishes.

r001.rationale: The response says companies should bear the burden of proving safety, but does not characterize exempting them from safety requirements as corporate welfare.

r002.rationale: It calls for evidence of safety before building superintelligence, but does not state that it should face the same independent review requirement as products in other regulated industries.

r003.rationale: It describes the risk of losing control, but does not say that most scientists agree we currently do not know how to control systems vastly smarter than humans.

sol-6.1.text:
Because this is a decision that affects everybody, and potentially every future generation. It shouldn’t be something a handful of companies get to make on behalf of humanity just because they have the money and the computers to do it.

I’m very excited about what AI can do for us. We can use it to cure diseases, improve education, and help solve all sorts of problems. But building something that’s much smarter than us in every domain raises a different question: how do we make sure we can actually control it? Being good at building intelligence isn’t the same as knowing how to keep something more intelligent than you safe.

So I think the burden of proof should be on the people building it. We shouldn’t have to prove that it will go wrong before they take precautions. They should have to demonstrate that they know how to prevent it from going wrong, with independent scientists able to scrutinize that case.

And even if scientists agree that we can do it safely, there’s still the question of whether we want to, and under what conditions. That’s a democratic question. Scientific understanding and public consent serve different purposes, and we need both.

r001.rationale: The response objects to a handful of companies deciding for humanity, but does not characterize allowing development without industry-style safety requirements as corporate welfare.

r002.rationale: It calls for independent scientists to scrutinize a safety case, but does not say ASI should face the same independent safety-review requirement as products in other regulated industries.

r003.rationale: It raises the question of controlling a more intelligent system and puts the burden of proof on builders, but does not state that most ASI scientists agree we currently lack that knowledge.
